lead: Fly-by-wire (FBW) replaces the mechanical link between cockpit and surface with wires, sensors and computers. The pilot moves a sidestick or column; gyros, accelerometers and air data measure the aircraft; redundant flight control computers use control laws to command hydraulic or electro-hydrostatic actuators. Fly-by-light (FBL) keeps the same chain but carries the signals over optical fibre. FBW is used on modern airliners and fighters because it saves weight, removes rigging and friction, and allows envelope protection and relaxed static stability.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for powered actuation and Chapter 1.4 for artificial feel.

blocks.text: In a mechanical system the pilot's hand supplies the command and the rod or cable carries it. In FBW the command becomes an electrical signal. A sidestick or column has position sensors; rate gyros measure body angular rates p, q and r (roll, pitch and yaw rates in degrees per second); accelerometers measure normal acceleration n<sub>z</sub> in g; air data gives airspeed V, dynamic pressure q<sub>bar</sub> and angle of attack α. These signals enter the flight control computer (FCC). The pilot never pushes the surface directly; the FCC decides how much surface deflection gives the commanded motion.

items: Pilot input: sidestick position gives a demand, for example a pitch rate in degrees per second.
Sensors: gyros, accelerometers and air data measure the actual motion and air state.
FCC: three or four independent lanes compute the same command; a voter compares lanes and rejects a disagreeing lane.
Actuator: the FCC sends a command to a servo actuator, usually powered by hydraulic pressure; an electro-hydrostatic actuator has its own electric pump.
Surface: the actuator moves the aileron, elevator or rudder; the resulting motion is fed back by the sensors.

blocks.text: A control law is the formula or table that turns pilot and sensor inputs into actuator commands. A rate command law commands pitch rate, roll rate or yaw rate; the FCC compares commanded rate with measured rate and drives the surface until the error is small. For pitch, the C* law blends pitch rate and normal acceleration: at low speed it behaves like a rate command, at high speed it limits load factor. This gives consistent handling across the flight envelope.

items: Normal mode: all protections active: stall, overspeed, bank and load-factor limits.
Alternate mode: some protections lost; control laws simplified.
Direct mode: pilot command goes to the actuator with minimal feedback; no envelope protection.

blocks.text: FBW saves weight by deleting cables, pulleys, turnbuckles and rigging. It removes friction and backlash. The FCC can add envelope protection, carefree handling, gust alleviation and relaxed static stability, which allows a smaller tail. The cost is dependence on electric power, computers and validated software; lightning and electromagnetic interference (EMI) need protection.

Early FBW was analog. Digital FBW samples signals and runs software, so it can self-check, schedule gains by software, run built-in test (BIT), and grow by software change. Redundancy is by lanes, not by making one lane perfect. With three lanes, two can outvote one; with four, a failed lane can be isolated. The worked example shows why: three lanes at 1 × 10⁻⁴ failures per hour give 1 × 10⁻¹² per hour for all three failing, below the usual 1 × 10⁻⁹ per hour catastrophic target.

blocks.where: p is the failure probability of one lane in one flight hour; k is the number of independent lanes.

blocks.text: Fly-by-light replaces the copper signal wires with optical fibre. It is immune to EMI, has no ground loops, cannot cause a spark at a fuel tank, is light and has high bandwidth. Problems are mechanical: fibre has a minimum bending radius, every connector loses optical power, and the optical power budget must close. FBL still uses hydraulic or electric power at the actuator.

examples.question: A digital FBW computer has three independent lanes. Each lane has a failure rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour. (a) Find the probability that all three lanes fail in one flight hour. (b) Repeat with a fourth independent lane. Assume failures are independent and the aircraft needs at least one lane.
steps: Let p = 1 × 10⁻⁴ per hour be the failure probability of one lane in one hour. Independence means multiply probabilities.
(a) For three lanes: P₃ = p × p × p = p³ = (1 × 10⁻⁴)³ = 1 × 10⁻¹² per hour.
(b) For four lanes: P₄ = p⁴ = (1 × 10⁻⁴)⁴ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁶ per hour.
The all-lanes-fail event is not the same as a catastrophic event; voting and isolation reduce it further. Both values are below 1 × 10⁻⁹ per hour.

traps: FBW removes the mechanical linkage, not hydraulic power; actuators still need hydraulic or electric power.
Artificial feel remains: sidestick springs and Q-feel create stick force, not airload feedback through cables.
Digital FBW is not just analog FBW with a computer: sampling, software validation, built-in test and gain scheduling are part of the design.
Fly-by-light is not wireless: optical fibre carries signals, while actuator power still comes by wire or hydraulic line.
Voting lanes improve availability; the usual design answer is not one perfect lane but independent lanes with comparison and isolation.

quiz.a: It replaces the mechanical linkage between cockpit and surface with electrical signals, sensors, computers and actuators; hydraulic power may remain.

quiz.q: Why does a FBW aircraft still need artificial feel?
quiz.a: The pilot no longer feels airloads through a mechanical link, so springs, Q-feel or a sidestick gradient must create stick force that rises with speed and deflection.

quiz.q: A lane fails at 2 × 10⁻⁵ per hour. Give the all-three-lanes failure probability for three independent lanes.
Why are three or four lanes used instead of one highly reliable lane?
quiz.a: Independent lanes with voting isolate a failed lane and prevent a single fault from commanding the surface. The probability of all lanes failing falls as p<sup>k</sup>; software and power still need protection.

quiz.q: Name two normal-mode protections and state what direct mode gives up.
quiz.a: Stall and overspeed protection, or bank and load-factor limits. Direct mode gives up envelope protection and much feedback; pilot command goes more directly to the actuator.

quiz.q: Give two reasons fly-by-light suits fuel tanks and two optical problems.
quiz.a: No spark hazard and immunity to EMI and ground loops. Problems: minimum bend radius and connector or optical power loss; the optical power budget must close.

quiz.q: State two advantages of digital over analog FBW.
quiz.a: Self-checking and built-in test; software gain scheduling. Software growth and fault isolation are also easier.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, FBW design is tied to systems safety and software assurance; FBL appears in research and some specialised aircraft because of EMI and fuel-tank safety.
